query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under tribo-corrosion conditions, the primary driver of accelerated material loss in high-entropy alloys is the repeated mechanical disruption of the protective passive layer, causing periodic exposure of fresh, reactive surfaces that rapidly corrode and deepen mechanical wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase or near-single-phase high-entropy alloy with a well-formed passive film on a polished surface prepared for tribological testing.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust normal load and solution pH in a pin-on-disc tribo-corrosion test while monitoring wear and electrochemical response in real time.
generation.conditions: Normal loads spanning low (e.g., 5 N) to high (e.g., 50 N) and solutions of varying pH (e.g., strongly acidic, neutral, and alkaline), with consistent sliding speed, contact geometry, and test temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamic formation, breakdown, and re-passivation of the oxide/passive layer on the alloy’s contact surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: Elevated normal loads and acidic conditions intensify both mechanical disruption of near-surface oxide layers and localized electrochemical activity, allowing corrosive species to access the exposed metal. This accelerates local dissolution and fosters debris formation, which in turn enhances subsequent abrasive wear and further disrupts the developing passive film.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline measurement under mild load and neutral pH, each increment in normal load and lowering of pH will significantly increase total material loss (>2× at highest loading/lowest pH). Separating mechanical wear (with no corrosive electrolyte) and electrochemical corrosion (with no mechanical contact) would each yield distinctly lower degradation rates than the coupled tribo-corrosion scenario.
generation.baseline: Pin-on-disk tests under near-neutral pH and minimal load, showing limited oxide film disruption and lower total material loss rates.
generation.boundary: In highly alkaline environments or under very low load, the synergy between wear and corrosion is minimized because stable passivation films persist. At extremely high loads or strongly acidic media, mechanical and corrosive damage is dominated by direct mechanical failure or uniform corrosion rather than synergy.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative estimates of the increase in wear volume and corrosion current density at each load/pH are not firmly established from the available data and require further direct measurement.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct identical tribo-corrosion tests in which one group uses an unprotected surface while another is pre-coated with a stable, artificially grown oxide film that is less prone to mechanical disruption. Continuously monitor open-circuit potential and sliding friction under the same load and environment conditions for both groups.
measurements: Open-circuit potential and real-time polarization curves
Surface morphology and passive film characterization (SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the group with a more durable, artificially stabilized passive film displays the same or higher total material loss compared with the unprotected group, this would contradict the hypothesis that repeated disruption of the protective layer is driving increased degradation.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe challenge of cavitation erosion (CE) in flow-handling components of marine engineering has promoted the development of advanced materials due to safety incidents and economic costs. High entropy alloys (HEAs), known for high hardness and corrosion resistance, emerge as promising candidates. This paper delved into the CE characteristics of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA when subjected to the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, elucidating the synergistic effect of CE-corrosion. The quantitative analysis revealed that CE-corrosion synergy contributed 48.02% to total CE mass loss, primarily attributed to corrosion-induced CE damage. Meanwhile, electrochemical noise (EN) was utilized to reveal the corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution combined with the morphologies observation and surface roughness. Extended CE time compromised the corrosion resistance of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA and diminished the impact of selective phase corrosion on the surface. Eventually, the CE damage mechanism of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA was revealed based on pertinent experimental findings.
